📌 Decentralized Identifiers (DIDs): Portable IDs for Web3

Main Points
⏺ DIDs are identifiers you control, not usernames owned by platforms
⏺ They can link to verifiable credentials like diplomas or KYC checks
⏺ This post explains how DIDs help build portable identity across apps

1️⃣ What Is a DID — a standardized identifier tied to keys you own, not to an email, phone number, or single company.
2️⃣ Verifiable Credentials — organizations can sign claims about you (for example, “passed KYC”, “finished course”) that you can present elsewhere.
3️⃣ User Control — you decide when and where to share proofs instead of giving every app full personal data.
4️⃣ Interoperability — multiple dApps, wallets, and even Web2 services can recognize the same DID as “you”.
5️⃣ Privacy Angle — combined with zero-knowledge proofs, DIDs can prove facts (age, residency, reputation) without revealing raw documents.

Final Thoughts

Decentralized identifiers turn identity from siloed accounts into something you own and reuse — a core building block for Web3 logins and reputation.

Senate vs. Trump: Iran Edition

Washington finally did what it does best: pass something “historic” that changes absolutely nothing. 

Three weeks after slapping Trump in the House, the Senate joined the therapy session and voted to order U.S. troops out of the Iran theater within 30 days — unless Congress blesses more war. 

The resolution is legally toothless, pure stage prop, but it sends one clear message: when the White House asks for another 80 billion for this adventure right before midterms, the answer will come with a calculator and a lawyer attached. Even Trump’s own party is starting to check the receipts.

Trump, of course, says Iran is “on the brink of surrender,” “ready to give us almost anything,” and now “has enormous respect” for America and, naturally, for its president. 

According to his version, the Senate just handed “aid and comfort to the enemy” with a “meaningless vote at a terrible time,” sabotaged by “four failing Republicans.” 

Somewhere in this script, Tehran — supposedly a regime seconds away from collapse — still has enough free time to consult psychologists about his tweet storms and to read “The Art of the Deal” like it’s a Pentagon field manual.

On paper, this is a constitutional drama about war powers; in reality, it is a custody battle over narrative. Trump sells the war as a discount victory: no new authorization, no clear end state, just faith in his personal brand scaring Iran into submission. 

Congress wants to pretend it didn’t sign the checks while the missiles were already in the air. The Pentagon keeps flying, the lawyers keep hedging, and everyone insists they’re defending “the troops” while using them as leverage in a budget fight.

The grotesque part is how both sides weaponize fear and ego in the same breath. Trump claims anyone voting to limit him is feeding the enemy. 

The Senate claims anyone trusting him with open‑ended war is betraying the republic. 

Iran, allegedly “about to fall,” turns into the world’s most overbooked therapist, diagnosing the American president while dodging drones.
